title: Can xswap release metadata after memory pressure?
subtitle: Structural campaign — allocation, tail reclamation and the lifetime blocker

verdict.headline: Promising reclamation, little RAM saved; a lifetime race blocks promotion

tiles.label: Tail-cache reclaim
tiles.note: High retention disappears in the primary workload.

tiles.label: Low-first allocation
tiles.note: High retention remains; selection adds lock work.

blocks.takeaway: Before: memory pressure leaves metadata behind

blocks.text: Xswap tracks pages with cluster descriptors. Shrink releases only a contiguous free tail. High cache-only slots can pin it. Hypothesis: better placement or blocker reclamation releases metadata.

blocks.takeaway: Allocation and metadata retirement surround the existing storage path

blocks.text: Application and backend roles stay unchanged. Metadata savings leave RAM for useful work, but are small here. Low-first adds lock work; tail-cache risks later swap-out I/O and more frequent retirement.

blocks.takeaway: Low-first: select a lower slot without moving live pages
Tail-cache: clear blockers before the existing tail shrink

blocks.text: Candidates are independent. Tail-cache v2 includes the verified assertion fix. Internal helper retries prevent a strict runtime bound.

blocks.takeaway: Tail-cache reclaim removes the high-retention regime in this workload
blocks.note: Each dot is one boot: A baseline, B candidate. Fewer mapped clusters is better; this measures descriptors, not total RAM.

blocks.takeaway: High retention can return after another pressure cycle
blocks.note: Mapped clusters; lower is better. Second pressure is diagnostic.

blocks.text: Low-first is inconclusive. Repeated pressure can leave new blockers after the last trigger. A source-level descriptor retirement race blocks promotion.

sections.title: Repair lifetime safety before pursuing the mechanism

blocks.takeaway: Next steps depend on passing the preceding safety check

blocks.text: Require baseline race reproduction and repair success. Retest with delayed retry; high retention would weaken the finding. Sanitizers, failure injection, confirmation and holdout remain missing. Warning failures are retained.

sections.title: What changed
sections.lead: Two independent mechanism candidates on the instrumented baseline, plus one assertion fix.

blocks.takeaway: Low-first changes where slots land; tail-cache clears cache-only blockers before shrink
xs-lowfree-v1: move the lowest free cluster to the list head
xs-tailcache-v2: bounded cache-only reclaim before tail shrink (+ assertion fix)

sections.title: How it was measured
sections.lead: AB/BA pairs, 10 per backend per candidate, after 8 A/A calibration boots.

blocks.takeaway: The score is read after the first settle; a second pressure cycle is diagnostic only

sections.title: What the data shows
sections.lead: Every boot is one dot; 219 clusters is the low regime.

blocks.takeaway: Tail-cache v2 settled at 219 clusters in 20/20 boots; its baseline was high in 10/20
A second pressure cycle brings the high regime back on both sides (zswap re-settle high: candidate 2/10, baseline 4/10)
In a high boot, PTE references stop at cluster 100; a few cache-only slots pin the tail
Neither candidate moved first-access latency beyond run-to-run spread

sections.title: Why
sections.lead: Shrink only unmaps a contiguous free tail; one cache-only slot ends that tail.

blocks.takeaway: Cache-only blockers explain the regime; the RAM involved is descriptor pages only

blocks.text: Per-cluster tables are freed with the cluster; high boots kept 37–50 nonempty clusters versus 37 in low boots.

blocks.takeaway: Data gates pass; lifetime and sanitizer coverage do not
